summary: For ages 11–12, build the leap from the KS2 attract/repel rule to the abstract FIELD MODEL: a magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet where it exerts a force, revealed (not created) by a plotting compass or iron filings, and represented by directed field lines running north-seeking → south-seeking, continuous, never crossing, with closer spacing meaning stronger. Treatment is qualitative only (no field-strength numbers) and includes Earth-as-a-magnet, the compass and navigation. The anchor activity is a hands-on/screen field-MAPPING task where learners probe the space with a compass and assemble field lines themselves; a drawing/prediction activity assesses the examined competency; a reference layer consolidates vocabulary; and a narrowly scoped 3D exploration addresses the real 'field is only the flat pattern' misconception.
misconceptions: 'The field IS the iron filings / lines' — the lines are a representation; the field is a continuous region of force filling 3D space (IOP).
'The field exists only at the poles' or 'lines come out of the centre of the magnet' (Oak).
Drawing field lines that cross, or that have no direction/arrows.
Conflating the magnetic field with the gravitational or electric field because all 'act at a distance' (IOP; Bradamante & Viennot).
'Magnets need air/a medium to work' — the force acts through a vacuum (IOP).
Pole-labelling/reversal errors in attraction-repulsion diagrams (KS3 assessment analysis); carried-over 'all metals are magnetic / aluminium is magnetic'.

activities.title: Map the field with a plotting compass
steps: Place a plotting compass far from any magnet and note that it settles pointing north.

Position a bar magnet, then move the compass step-by-step to many positions around it; at each position draw a small arrow pointing the way the needle's NORTH-SEEKING end points — this is the field direction, running outward from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole.
Join the arrows to trace continuous field lines, working outward from one pole and around to the other.

Deliberately place the compass out to the SIDE of the magnet (not just near the poles) and record which way the needle points compared with when the magnet was absent. Near the magnet the needle lines up with the magnet's field, but with some magnet orientations that direction can match its original northward direction, so also try turning the magnet.
Overlay or compare an iron-filings pattern on the same magnet, noting that filings show shape/strength while the compass shows direction — two readings of one field.
Bring a second magnet nearby and re-map a few points to see how the whole pattern changes (like poles push lines apart, opposite poles link them).
activities.insight: The field is a continuous region of force filling the space all around the magnet, not something that exists only at the poles or only where a line is drawn; the compass and filings merely PROBE it. Direction and strength are two readings of one invisible field.

activities.title: Draw, predict and apply the field-line rules
steps: Trace a field line through a marked point on a bar-magnet diagram, and at several marked positions draw the direction a compass needle would point.
Predict which way a compass will swing when placed at a given point near the magnet, then check against a plotted pattern.
Decide whether drawn field lines obey the rules: Do any cross? Do they carry arrows? Does spacing show strength?
Label the poles of a magnet from an unlabelled field pattern.
Predict-and-explain (predict, observe, explain): a compass far from magnets points north; predict what happens as a bar magnet is brought alongside it, and WHY, before testing.
activities.insight: Field-line drawing is a precise skill governed by rules (continuous, arrowed north→south, never crossing, spacing = strength), and the learner can predict a compass's behaviour from the field rather than treating it as a passive pointer.

activities.title: Earth as a magnet and the compass for navigation
steps: Draw the Earth as a bar magnet with a compass needle aligning to its field.
Explain why a compass needle's SAME end always turns to point north, in terms of the needle being a tiny magnet aligning with Earth's field.
Reason about transfer: if you took the compass to Australia, would the same end still point north? Why?

Discuss the enrichment point: the Earth's magnetic pole near geographic north behaves like a magnetic south-type pole, so the needle's north pole is attracted to it (opposites attract) — flagged as enrichment, not required.
activities.insight: A compass works because the needle is itself a small magnet that aligns with Earth's magnetic field (when away from other magnets and iron), which is why the same end consistently points (magnetic) north and the compass can be used for navigation.

activities.title: Reference layer: the field-line rules at a glance
steps: Consult a finished, labelled bar-magnet field diagram and reveal, region by region, the rules: lines run N→S, closer spacing = stronger, field strongest at the poles.
Reveal the Earth/compass link: Earth acts like a bar magnet and the compass needle aligns with its field.
Use this as a vocabulary and rule check-reference alongside the mapping activity.
activities.insight: Consolidates the correct vocabulary and the field-line rules as a quick reference to support, not replace, hands-on probing.

activities.title: The field in three dimensions (narrow complement)
steps: Move a compass or sensor through the space around a magnet at different heights and positions — above, below and to the sides — not just in the flat tabletop plane.

Record how the needle responds at each height and position close to the magnet (the effect weakens with distance), concluding the field occupies a VOLUME around the magnet, not only the flat textbook pattern.
Relate the 3D volume back to the 2D field-line diagram, recognising the diagram as one slice through the full field.
activities.insight: The magnetic field is genuinely three-dimensional — it surrounds the magnet in every direction — and the familiar 2D field-line diagram is one plane through that volume.

checkQuestion: A compass needle settles pointing north wherever you put it in the room. What is making the needle point that way — and why does the SAME end always end up pointing north?
checkAnswer: The Earth has its own magnetic field. The compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with that field, so its north-seeking (north) pole always turns toward Earth's magnetic north. The same end points north because it is that end's north pole being pulled along the field toward Earth's magnetic north (which is actually a magnetic south-type pole, so opposites attract).
